newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Copper jolted by inventory increase.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Copper jolted by inventory increase.

text.p: Recent firmness in copper prices took a knock on Wednesday as the London Metal Exchange (LME) revealed that stocks in its warehouses rose by nearly 12 percent the previous day.
Among other commodities, weather watchers in Chicago pushed grain prices lower while coffee prices saw a brief respite from Tuesday's relentless selling, and investment funds moved into sugar.

Daily returns submitted by LME approved warehouses showed that copper inventories on Tuesday were up by just over 17,000 tonnes to 160,325 tonnes due to metal being shipped into warehouses in Singapore and the U.S.
"This certainly unsettled the market....and I think there is more to come," said analyst Angus MacMillan at broker Billiton Metals.

Analysts reckon that the rise was the start of upto 50,000 tonnes that could be arriving in LME warehouses in the near future due to slower Asian demand and a summer holiday slow-down in Europe and the U.S.
New mine capacity will also result in higher copper stocks, they said.
On the LME the benchmark three months delivery copper price dropped around $30 a tonne on the news before recovering to end the day at $2,267, down $11.
The premium for prompt delivery, recently very tight, dropped around $70 to $200 a tonne.

In Chicago, forecasts for showers this weekend in key U.S. corn and soyabean growing states hit most grain contracts on the Board of Trade, relieving the recent upward pressure put on prices by a dry spell.
At midday September wheat and corn were down around six cents a bushel at $3.33 and $2.50, and soyabeans were over 20 cents down with August futures indicated around $7.52 a bushel.
Coffee prices attempted to stabilise after their fall of over ten percent on Tuesday prompted by fund liquidation finding buyers with little reason to provide much resistance.
Shrinking chances of a severe frost in Brazil and rising U.S. coffee bean stocks kept them away.
But although these downward pressures would probably remain on the market, the funds did not press as much today and prices rallied by around $30 a tonne in London.
In the sugar market a firming in prices was prompted by talk in Europe of crop damage caused by Polish floods, and of Russian buying interest.
The rise triggered off investment fund interest, particularly in U.S. futures, and resulted in strong gains over the day.
